### AI for journal entries and bank reconciliation: automate it safely
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/ai-journal-entries-bank-reconciliation/
Published: 2026-10-14

AI automates journal entries and bank reconciliation by predicting how documents should be coded, matching bank transactions to open invoices, bills and payments, and drafting entries for review. It should handle high-volume, well-evidenced items such as customer receipts and bank charges, while a named person approves judgemental entries, owns matching tolerances and reviews every unmatched or written-off difference.

- Automate by evidence: the stronger the external proof for an entry, the more the machine can prepare it.
- In Odoo 20, entries that hit bank accounts must originate from bank transactions.
- Matching tolerances and write-off accounts are control settings with an owner, not user preferences.
- Prove the automation on a closed month before any live use, comparing difference by difference.

Every finance manager knows the suspense account that grows a little each month. A customer pays three invoices in one transfer and the bank deducts a charge; the receipt does not equal any single invoice, so it is parked. A vendor bill is coded the way the last one was, whether or not the last one was right. By year end the reconciliation agrees, but nobody can explain a handful of lines without opening old emails.

This is where AI earns its place in accounting: high volumes of entries whose correct treatment is mostly evident from the documents. It is also where careless automation does the most damage, because a wrong match clears a balance that should have stayed open. This article, part of our practical guide to AI in accounting, sets out how to automate both safely.

#### What does automating journal entries with AI mean?

AI journal entry automation is the use of learned patterns and document reading to prepare entries and reconciliations that a person then reviews and approves, rather than keying each one by hand. In practice it combines four layers, and it helps to know which one you are looking at:

- Rules: reconciliation models that propose or book a fixed treatment, such as a recurring bank charge. Available in recent Odoo versions; confirm their behaviour in your 20 database.
- Extraction: bill digitization (OCR) that reads vendor documents, which in recent Odoo versions consumes IAP credits.
- Prediction: according to Odoo’s 20 release notes, when a bill is encoded manually or by import, Odoo suggests the product, account, tax, analytic and vehicle values from bill history and the label.
- Agents: the release notes also describe AI agents that can create and update records, including from an uploaded instruction file such as a PDF, and that can be triggered by automated or scheduled actions.

#### How does AI match bank transactions?

Bank matching is a search for the open item that best explains a statement line. Good matching works in a fixed order, from strongest evidence to weakest, and stops at the first confident answer:

1. Exact reference: the payment reference on the statement equals an invoice or payment number.
2. Partner and amount: the counterparty is recognised and the amount equals one open item.
3. Combination: the amount equals the sum of several open items of the same partner.
4. Tolerance: the amount differs from an open item by less than an agreed tolerance, and the difference goes to a defined write-off account.
5. No match: the line stays open for a person, with the candidates the system considered.

Odoo 20 formalises much of this. According to Odoo’s 20 release notes, matching rules for invoices and bills now support a payment tolerance and a matching order, you can run Auto Reconciliation manually, and a write-off created during reconciliation can carry an analytic distribution. The AI-powered financial insights feature can review suspected reconciliation errors and return findings and recommendations, working only from the accounting data in your database.

##### A worked example without amounts

Take the customer who pays three invoices in one transfer with a bank charge deducted. Steps 1 and 2 fail: no single reference, no single invoice amount. Step 3 finds the three invoices whose total is close to the receipt. Step 4 accepts the shortfall only if it is within the tolerance the controller set, and books it to the bank charges account with the customer’s analytic tag. If the shortfall is larger, the line stays open, because a customer short-payment is a collection issue, not a bank charge. The rule protects the receivable ledger from being quietly written down.

#### What does Odoo 20 change in bank and entry controls?

The most important change is not AI at all. Odoo’s 20 release notes state that entries impacting bank accounts must originate from bank transactions, with clearer statement validation. A manual journal entry straight to the bank account, the classic way a ledger drifts from the statement, is no longer the normal path. Alongside it, the notes list a bank reconciliation summary report of reconciled and unreconciled items at period end, statement batching and quick reconciliation shortcuts, red and yellow duplicate warnings on invoices and bills, a payment wizard that detects pending payments to prevent double payment, and hashing of cash journal entries on reconciliation. We cover the payables side in Odoo 20 bank reconciliation and bill payments.

#### Which entries should AI draft, and which should it never touch?

Our decision rule is simple: automate in proportion to the external evidence behind the entry. The table applies it to the entries a typical finance team posts every month.

| Entry type | Evidence available | Automation level | Control |
| Bank charges and recurring fees | Bank statement line | Rule or match, auto-proposed | Monthly review of the charges account by the controller |
| Customer receipts | Statement line plus open invoice | AI match within tolerance | Weekly list of tolerance write-offs, reviewed and signed |
| Vendor bills with stable history | Vendor document plus purchase order | Predicted lines, person confirms | Override rate tracked; coding policy beats history |
| Accruals and provisions | Estimates and judgement | AI drafts the schedule only | Preparer and approver both named; reversed next period |
| Closing adjustments | Analysis, often off-system | Draft with cited records | Second approver above materiality |
| Correcting entries | The original error and its source | Agent drafts a reversal and a new entry | No deletion; approver is not the preparer |
| Manual entries to bank accounts | None beyond the entry itself | Not allowed in Odoo 20 | Bank entries come from bank transactions |

Notice what the bottom rows share: the less the external evidence, the more the AI is limited to drafting, and the more the approval depends on your ISA 320 materiality threshold.

#### What controls keep automated entries auditable?

The existing bank reconciliation controls still apply: an independent reviewer, aged reconciling items, no plugging differences. Automation adds five of its own:

- A distinct system user for every agent or automation, so the audit trail shows the machine as preparer and a person as approver. How that fits your access matrix is covered in AI, segregation of duties and internal controls.
- Tolerances, write-off accounts and matching order owned by the controller and changed only through a logged approval.
- Corrections by reversal, never by deletion, so the original AI proposal remains visible.
- Every AI explanation of a match or entry cites the records it used; one that cites nothing is rejected. This is the principle behind evidence or silence.
- Lock dates on closed periods, a long-standing Odoo control, so no automation can reach back into a signed-off month.

> Automate the match, never the explanation of a difference.

#### How do you know the automation is working?

Measure it like any other control, monthly and on the full population rather than a sample. Four indicators are enough to start:

- Auto-match share: the percentage of statement lines matched without manual intervention, tracked by matching rule.
- Tolerance write-offs: count and trend of differences booked under tolerance. A rising count is a collection or pricing issue, not an efficiency gain.
- Prediction override rate: how often people change a predicted bill line. High rates on one vendor point to bad history.
- Reversals of automated entries: each one is a finding about a rule, a model or a document.

These indicators feed straight into the close; see AI in the monthly close and financial reporting for how they fit the close calendar.

#### What will an auditor test?

ISA 240 requires the auditor to test the appropriateness of journal entries, and the population now includes entries prepared by software. Expect an auditor to ask for the list of automation users and rules, the approval log for changes to tolerances, and a full-population extract of entries by preparer. The patterns we look for in our own continuous-audit work are familiar: duplicate and near-duplicate payments, manual entries posted late at month-end in round amounts, and approvals outside the approval matrix. A flagged entry is a question for management, not proof of error or fraud; AI-based fraud detection explains how to treat flags. Testing every entry rather than a sample is covered in from sampling to full-population testing.

#### Where to start on Monday

1. Export last month’s bank statement lines and your reconciliation, and count lines matched manually, lines parked in suspense and lines older than thirty days.
2. List every reconciliation model and matching rule in your database, with who created it and what write-off account it uses.
3. Set a tolerance in writing, approved by the finance manager, before enabling any automatic matching.
4. Run automatic matching on a copy of the closed month and compare each match with what your team did. Every disagreement is either a rule to fix or a human error found.
5. Go live on one bank account, review the tolerance write-off list weekly for a full quarter, then extend.

If you are on Odoo, confirm each feature above in your own 20 database and edition before you design around it. Reconciliation rules and approval paths are design decisions for any Odoo ERP implementation, not settings to leave at default, and our MFT Intelligence agents draft correcting entries that a named, registered person approves; nothing is auto-posted. For the full rollout sequence, see the step-by-step guide to AI accounting on Odoo 20.

Q: Can AI do bank reconciliation automatically?
A: AI can propose most matches automatically when the evidence is strong: a matching reference, a known partner and an equal amount, or a combination within an approved tolerance. It should not resolve unexplained differences. Those stay open for a person to investigate, and a reviewer who does not handle payments signs off the reconciliation.

Q: What is a payment tolerance in bank reconciliation?
A: A payment tolerance is the largest difference between a bank receipt and an open invoice that the system may accept as a match, booking the difference to a defined write-off account. It is a control setting: the controller should own it, approve changes in writing and review the resulting write-offs regularly.

Q: Should AI post journal entries without approval?
A: No. AI should prepare entries and a named person should approve them, with a second approver above the materiality threshold for judgemental entries. Corrections should be made by reversal, not deletion, so the audit trail shows both what the machine proposed and what a person decided.

Q: What does Odoo 20 change for bank entries?
A: According to Odoo’s 20 release notes, entries that affect bank accounts must originate from bank transactions, with clearer statement validation. The notes also add a reconciliation summary report at period end, matching rules with payment tolerance and matching order, and the ability to run Auto Reconciliation manually.

Q: How do I test AI reconciliation before going live?
A: Run it on a copy of a month you have already closed and compare every match with your team’s reconciliation. Each disagreement is either a rule to correct or a human error the automation found. Go live on one bank account first and review the tolerance write-offs weekly for a quarter.

Sources:
- Odoo, "Odoo 20 Release Notes" (Sept 2026): https://www.odoo.com/odoo-20-release-notes

### AI financial fraud detection: red flags, models and limits
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/ai-financial-fraud-detection/
Published: 2026-10-14

AI financial fraud detection scores every transaction in the ledger against red-flag patterns, such as duplicate payments, near-duplicate vendors, approvals outside the matrix and round manual entries posted late at month-end, and routes the highest scores to a person. A flag is a lead to investigate with evidence, never proof of fraud or of a misstatement.

- AI fraud detection scores every transaction and ranks the riskiest for human review.
- A flag is a lead to test with evidence, never proof of fraud or a misstatement.
- The ACFE’s 2026 report puts the median time to detection at 12 months; ongoing monitoring shortens it.
- Odoo 20 adds preventive duplicate and payment checks; looking back across history still needs a review process.

Picture the payables run at quarter-end. Two queued bills carry the same vendor invoice number with one character changed. A vendor created last month shares a bank account with an old one. A round manual journal entry lands on the final evening of the month, posted by a user who rarely posts manual entries. None of this is hidden. It sits in the ledger, and in most companies nobody looks until the annual audit.

The ACFE’s Occupational Fraud 2026 report, built on 2,402 cases from 143 countries and territories, found that the median fraud runs 12 months before it is detected, and that tips, not controls, remain the top detection method at 43% of cases. AI does not change who commits fraud. It changes how quickly the ledger can tell you that something does not fit. Below: what the models test, how to triage their output, and the line every finance team must hold: a flag is not proof.

#### What is AI financial fraud detection?

AI financial fraud detection is the use of rules, statistical models and language models to score every transaction in a company’s books for patterns associated with fraud or error, so that people review the riskiest items first instead of a random few. Three parts of that definition matter. It covers every transaction, which is why it belongs with full-population testing rather than sampling. It produces a score, not a verdict. And it ends with a person, because a model can rank but cannot judge intent.

It is also wider than fraud. The pattern behind a fraudulent payment equally fits an honest duplicate, a cut-off error or a misconfigured tax. Most flags turn out to be error, which is useful: both usually live in the same weak control.

#### Which red flags can AI test across the whole ledger?

These red flags recur in MFT’s continuous-audit work. Each is testable from ERP data and points back to a control, where the lasting fix belongs.

| Red flag | What the model compares | First test by a reviewer | Control it points to |
| Duplicate and near-duplicate payments | Vendor, amount, date and invoice reference, including near-identical references | Pull both bills and payments; confirm two real deliveries exist | Duplicate checks at bill entry and the three-way match |
| Near-duplicate vendors | Names, tax numbers, bank accounts and addresses across the vendor master | Trace who created each record and who approved the bank details | Approval of vendor master changes |
| Approvals outside the approval matrix | Approver and value band against the approved matrix | Check whether the approver held that authority on that date | Approval limits and segregation of duties |
| Round manual entries posted late at month-end | Entry source, posting time, user, and how round the figure is | Read the support; confirm the business reason | Journal entry review before the close |
| Cut-off errors | Delivery, receipt and invoice dates against the period posted | Match the goods movement to the accounting date | Period-end cut-off procedure and lock dates |
| Inventory valuation drift | Unit cost movement against purchase history and the valuation method | Recompute the cost of the items that moved | Costing review and the valuation close |

#### How do the models behind a fraud flag work?

Three families of technique do the work; a credible setup uses all three.

##### Rules: the patterns you already know

Rules encode what an experienced auditor already looks for: the same vendor and reference twice, a payment approved by the person who created the vendor. They are transparent and easy to defend in a working paper, but find only what someone thought to write down.

##### Anomaly scoring: what does not fit

Anomaly models learn what normal looks like for each account, vendor or user and score departures: a user who never posts manual entries suddenly posting several, a vendor whose invoice frequency doubles. They catch new patterns but also flag every legitimate business change, so their output needs triage, not trust.

##### Language models: reading the narrative

Language models read what numbers cannot: entry descriptions, bill labels, vendor names written in two scripts. Their known risk is stating things that are not in the data. That is why MFT’s agents work under the rule we call evidence or silence, set out in our article on AI provenance and the audit trail: a finding that does not cite the records it was drawn from is rejected, not reported.

#### What is a fraud flag not?

A flag is not proof of fraud. It is not proof of a misstatement either. It is a statement that a transaction differs from a pattern, and that the difference has an explanation someone has to find. Treating flags as accusations exposes honest staff to suspicion and teaches the organisation to argue with the system instead of using it.

> A flag is a question the ledger asks; only evidence can answer it.

Every flag should therefore close in one of three documented outcomes, with the evidence attached:

1. Explained: the reviewer found a legitimate reason (a split delivery, an agreed advance, a corrected bill) and attached the document that shows it.
2. Error or control gap: no fraud indicator, but a mistake or a weak control. It becomes an internal audit finding with an owner and a target date, rated by impact and likelihood.
3. Escalated: the explanation is missing, contradicts the documents, or comes only from the person under review. It goes to whoever owns fraud matters (often the audit committee chair, the owner or legal counsel), outside the reporting line involved, and the evidence is preserved before anyone is asked.

In the third case, do not confront, delete or quietly "fix" the entry. Corrections come later, by reversal, so the original record survives.

#### Why does detection speed matter so much?

Because time is what fraud needs. The ACFE’s 2026 report puts the median duration at 12 months before detection, the same figure as its 2024 report. More than half of the 2026 cases involved a lack of internal controls or an override of existing ones, and the controls associated with stronger outcomes (lower losses and faster detection) include proactive data monitoring, management review and surprise audits. An annual audit examines the year after it ends; as we argue in why the annual audit misses eleven months, that leaves the window open for most of the year.

Standards point the same way. ISA 240 requires the auditor to test the appropriateness of journal entries, and Principle 16 of COSO’s Internal Control, Integrated Framework expects ongoing evaluations, not only separate ones. A model that scores entries weekly is ongoing evaluation in practice; one that runs once a year is a better sampling tool.

#### What does Odoo 20 add for fraud prevention?

According to Odoo’s 20 release notes, several accounting changes make some red flags harder to create in the first place:

- Duplicate detection on invoices and bills with two warning levels: red for a highly likely duplicate, yellow for a potential one.
- A payment wizard that detects pending payments, to prevent the same bill being paid twice.
- Bank consistency: entries that affect bank accounts must originate from bank transactions, which closes the manual route into the bank balance.
- User group changes logged in the user’s chatter, so a temporary grant of rights before a sensitive posting leaves a trace.
- Hashing of cash journal entries on reconciliation.

These are preventive controls at entry. They do not look back across history, compare the vendor master for near-duplicates, or score a user against their own pattern. A yellow warning that staff learn to dismiss is no control at all. For the AI items in the release, see Odoo 20 AI features for accounting. Confirm each feature in your own database and edition before you design controls around it.

#### Where are the limits of AI fraud detection?

- Data: cash taken before it is recorded, or a side agreement with a vendor, leaves no line to score.
- Collusion: when requester and approver act together, every individual control passes. Testing pairs (requester with approver, buyer with vendor) lowers the odds but does not close the gap.
- False positives: flooded reviewers stop reading. Start with fewer, sharper tests.
- Override outside the system: an approval given by phone and keyed in later looks clean in the data.
- The tool itself: anything that drafts entries is a user and needs the same segregation and logging as a person.

None of these is a reason to wait. Pair the model with management review, surprise checks and an easy reporting channel, since more than half of tips come from employees.

#### Where should a finance team start on Monday?

1. For each red flag in the table above, name the preventive control and its owner.
2. Export one quarter of vendor bills, payments, the vendor master and manual journal entries. Run the duplicate payment, near-duplicate vendor and late round entry tests first; the same data also feeds daily matching, as described in automating journal entries and bank reconciliation with AI.
3. Agree the triage outcomes and the escalation owner before the first flag.
4. Tune for two or three cycles: retire noisy tests, tighten useful ones.
5. Move to weekly once triage keeps pace.

This is the approach behind seg-audit, MFT’s continuous audit platform. It reads the books straight from the ERP, read-only, scores every transaction by risk instead of sampling a few percent, links repeat findings to earlier ones, and no finding closes without a named, registered approver. The MFT Auditor agent drafts findings and corrections under the evidence-or-silence rule, and a person approves them. If you want an independent view of where your controls are thin, our internal audit service starts with exactly these tests.

Q: Can AI detect financial fraud on its own?
A: No. AI can score every transaction for patterns associated with fraud or error and rank the riskiest for review, but it cannot establish intent or confirm that fraud occurred. That takes a person examining source documents, explanations and context, and, where warranted, an investigation run by the right owner with the evidence preserved.

Q: What red flags does AI find most often in accounts payable?
A: Duplicate and near-duplicate payments, near-duplicate vendor records sharing a bank account or tax number, approvals outside the approval matrix, and bills recorded in the wrong period. Each can be tested from ERP data, and each traces back to a specific preventive control such as duplicate checks, vendor master approval or the three-way match.

Q: Does a fraud flag mean someone committed fraud?
A: No. A flag means a transaction departs from an expected pattern, and most flags turn out to be legitimate exceptions or honest errors. Each one should close as explained, as an error or control gap, or as escalated, with evidence attached. Nobody should be treated as a suspect on the strength of a score.

Q: How does AI fraud detection relate to ISA 240?
A: ISA 240 sets out the auditor’s responsibilities relating to fraud and requires testing the appropriateness of journal entries. Scoring every manual entry for risk factors such as timing, user and round figures gives the auditor and internal audit a full-population view to select from. The auditor’s judgment and documentation duties do not change.

Q: Does Odoo 20 have built-in fraud detection?
A: Odoo’s 20 release notes describe preventive checks rather than a fraud module: red and yellow duplicate warnings on invoices and bills, pending payment detection in the payment wizard, bank entries that must come from bank transactions, and logged user group changes. Analysis across history still needs a separate review process. Confirm each feature in your edition.

Sources:
- ACFE, "Occupational Fraud 2026: A Report to the Nations" (press release, 19 May 2026): https://www.acfe.com/about-the-acfe/newsroom-for-media/press-releases/press-release-detail?s=report-to-the-
- ACFE, "Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations" (report, 2024): https://www.acfe.com/en-us/-/media/files/acfe/pdfs/rttn/2024/2024-report-to-the-nations.pdf
- Odoo, "Odoo 20 Release Notes" (September 2026): https://www.odoo.com/odoo-20-release-notes

### AI in the month-end close and financial reporting: what to automate
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/ai-month-end-close-financial-reporting/
Published: 2026-10-14

AI helps the month-end close by doing the matching, reconciling, variance scanning and first-draft commentary that consume most of the close calendar, and by testing every entry before the period is locked. It should draft accruals, adjustments and explanations for a named person to approve, never post them, and every reported number must trace to cited records.

- Most close time goes on matching, chasing and explaining, which is where AI helps first.
- AI drafts adjustments and commentary; a named person approves, tiered by materiality.
- Every number in AI-written commentary must trace to records in the books, or it is struck out.
- Move matching and entry testing into the month so the close starts with exceptions only.

It is the third working day of the close. The bank still has unmatched lines from the second week of the month, the accrual for goods received but not yet billed lives in someone’s spreadsheet, and the management pack will go out with commentary written late at night by the person who also prepared the numbers. The close is rarely slow because the accounting is hard. It is slow because of matching, chasing and explaining, three kinds of work that AI handles well if the controls around it are designed first.

Finance teams are already moving. Gartner’s 2025 AI in Finance Survey found that 59% of finance leaders use AI in their finance function, against 58% in 2024 and 37% in 2023, and that adoption has levelled off, with complexity, data and talent cited as barriers. That figure covers the finance function broadly, not the close specifically, but the barriers it names are exactly the ones a close project meets.

#### What does AI in the month-end close mean?

AI in the month-end close is the use of matching models, anomaly tests and language models to prepare, check and explain a period’s numbers, while people approve every entry that changes the books. It is useful to split the close into three kinds of work, because AI plays a different role in each:

- Preparing: matching bank lines, reconciling balance sheet accounts, drafting accruals and adjustments.
- Checking: testing every manual entry, cut-off, valuation movements and unusual balances before the period is locked.
- Explaining: drafting variance commentary and the narrative of the management report.

The steps of a sound close do not change. Our month-end close checklist for Odoo sets them out; this article is about where AI fits inside them.

#### Which close tasks can AI do, and which must stay human?

The decision rule we apply: AI may propose anything, may check everything, and may change the books only through a draft that a named person approves. The matrix below applies it task by task.

| Close task | What AI does | What a person does | Evidence kept |
| Bank reconciliation | Proposes matches and lists unmatched lines, as described in automating bank reconciliation with AI | Approves matches and every write-off | Reconciled and unreconciled items at period end |
| Accruals for goods received not billed | Drafts the accrual from receipts with no bill, with a reversal date | Approves the estimate and the reversal | The receipt records the draft cites |
| Balance sheet account reconciliations | Compares ledger balances with subledgers and lists breaks | Resolves breaks and signs the reconciliation | Signed reconciliation with its support |
| Manual journal entry review | Scores every manual entry for timing, user, roundness and posting after cut-off | Investigates the high scores | Score, reviewer and outcome per entry |
| Inventory valuation close | Compares unit cost movements and drafts valuation adjustments | Approves valuation entries | Recomputed cost per item moved |
| Variance commentary | Drafts explanations that cite accounts and records | Edits and owns the narrative | Record references behind every figure |
| Period lock | Checks that preconditions are met: no unapproved drafts, no open breaks | Sets the lock date | Lock log and the checklist sign-off |

#### How does AI change the close calendar?

The largest gain does not come from doing close tasks faster on day 1. It comes from moving them out of the close window altogether.

##### During the month

If bank matching and manual entry scoring run daily, the close starts with a short list of exceptions instead of a month of raw transactions. The same scoring that supports AI-based fraud detection doubles as a close control: a round manual entry posted late on the last evening of the month is a classic finding in MFT’s continuous-audit work, and it is far easier to question on the day it is posted.

##### The first days of the close

AI drafts accruals, reclassifications and valuation adjustments, each with the records it relied on. The accountant’s job shifts from building entries to reviewing them, which is faster only if every draft shows its evidence.

##### Reporting

Once the trial balance is approved, AI drafts the variance commentary and the management report narrative. The controller edits. Nothing in the pack is a number the controller cannot trace.

#### Who approves what AI drafts?

Speed is worthless if it comes from skipping review. The approval design we use with clients has four rules:

1. Every draft carries the record references it was built from. A draft without them is returned, not reviewed.
2. Approval is tiered by the client’s ISA 320 materiality threshold: below it, one named approver; above it, a second approver. Our article on setting the materiality threshold explains how to fix it.
3. The person who requested or ran the AI task never approves its output, which is segregation of duties applied to AI agents.
4. Corrections are made by reversal, never by deleting or editing a posted entry, so the trail of what was proposed, approved and corrected survives.

> A close is fast when the evidence is ready, not when the approvals are skipped.

#### Can AI write the financial report commentary?

It can write the first draft, and it often writes it better than a tired controller at midnight. The danger is specific: a language model can produce a fluent sentence with a number that does not exist in the books. A practical tie-out test catches this before the report leaves the finance team:

1. Highlight every figure and percentage in the draft commentary.
2. Trace each one to the approved trial balance or the records the draft cites.
3. Strike out any figure that cannot be traced, and any sentence whose cause is asserted without a record behind it.
4. Keep the traced draft with the close file as evidence of review.

MFT’s agents apply the same rule automatically under the evidence-or-silence principle described in our article on AI provenance and the audit trail: a finding that cites nothing, or a number absent from the cited records, is rejected and shown struck through, never as a fact. The human tie-out remains, because the controller signs the pack, not the model.

#### What does Odoo 20 change for the close?

According to Odoo’s 20 release notes, several accounting changes touch the close directly:

- A bank reconciliation summary report listing reconciled and unreconciled transactions at period end, plus the option to run Auto Reconciliation manually.
- Bank consistency: entries affecting bank accounts must originate from bank transactions.
- Under perpetual valuation, accrual entries from the inventory valuation closing report post directly to the valuation account, and cost of goods sold is updated retroactively when cost changes after delivery. See the Odoo 20 inventory valuation changes.
- Exchange gains and losses consolidated into one line per invoice, and depreciation models that accept rates and decimals.
- Payment statuses renamed: "In Process" becomes "Paid" and "Paid" becomes "Reconciled", which affects saved filters and close reports.
- AI-powered financial insights: questions to the AI assistant about receivables, cash flow or reconciliation issues, answered solely from accounting data in your database, including a review of suspected reconciliation errors.

All AI features in Odoo 20 run on IAP credits billed per request and not included in any plan, so a daily AI routine has a running cost to budget. Lock dates, reconciliation models and Spreadsheet dashboards exist in recent Odoo versions; confirm how they behave in your 20 database before you build the close around them. The full AI map is in Odoo 20 AI features for accounting.

#### What can go wrong when AI enters the close?

- Automating a broken close: if the chart of accounts or cut-off rules are unclear, AI reproduces the confusion faster.
- Accepting matches in bulk: approval becomes a click, and the control disappears while the log says it happened.
- Drafts piling up: unapproved drafts at lock date mean the period closes on numbers nobody owns. Make "no open drafts" a lock precondition.
- Evidence in the wrong place: Odoo 20 keeps stored AI conversations up to 30 days after the last message, so anything that supports a closing entry belongs in the close file, not in a chat.

#### Where should you start this month?

1. Write your close calendar as a list of tasks with the working days each takes and who owns it.
2. Mark the tasks that are mostly matching, chasing or explaining. Those are the candidates.
3. Run AI in parallel for one close on two of them, without changing the official process, and compare its drafts with what your team posted.
4. Set the approval tiers and the lock preconditions before the AI output counts.
5. In the following close, move matching and entry scoring into the month, and keep commentary drafting for last.

This is the work our Virtual CFO agent does as a managed service: it reads the books through the API at query time, drafts analysis and adjustments that cite the records behind them, and leaves approval to a named person on the client’s side; nothing is auto-posted. For teams that also want an experienced finance lead around the close, our Virtual CFO service pairs that work with people who have closed books and signed reports themselves.

Q: Can AI close the books automatically?
A: No, and it should not. AI can match transactions, reconcile accounts, test entries and draft accruals, adjustments and commentary, but each change to the books should be a draft that a named person approves, with a second approver above the materiality threshold. The person who signs the financial statements remains accountable for them.

Q: Which month-end close tasks should be automated with AI first?
A: Start with tasks that are mostly matching and chasing: bank reconciliation, balance sheet account reconciliations and scoring every manual journal entry. They have clear evidence, measurable outcomes and low judgment. Leave estimates, valuation adjustments and report commentary until the approval tiers and the evidence rules have been proven in at least one close.

Q: Is AI-generated financial commentary reliable?
A: Only after a tie-out. A language model can write a fluent explanation containing a figure that is not in the books. Trace every number and percentage to the approved trial balance or cited records, strike anything that cannot be traced, and keep the traced draft in the close file as evidence of review.

Q: How should AI-drafted adjustments be approved?
A: Tie approval to materiality. Below the ISA 320 based threshold, one named approver signs; above it, a second approver is required. The person who ran the AI task never approves its output, every draft must cite the records it used, and corrections are made by reversal so the original entry and its history remain.

Q: What does Odoo 20 add to the month-end close?
A: Odoo’s 20 release notes list a bank reconciliation summary report at period end, a manual Auto Reconciliation option, bank entries that must come from bank transactions, inventory valuation accruals posting directly to the valuation account, and AI-powered financial insights that run on IAP credits. Confirm each item in your own database and edition.

- Odoo, "Odoo 20 Release Notes" (September 2026): https://www.odoo.com/odoo-20-release-notes

### Continuous auditing with AI vs traditional audit: side by side
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/continuous-auditing-ai-vs-traditional-audit/
Published: 2026-10-14

Continuous auditing with AI tests every transaction against defined rules shortly after it is posted, instead of testing a sample of a closed period months later. It shortens the time between an error and its detection and extends coverage to the whole population. It does not replace the external auditor’s opinion, professional judgement, or a named approver for each finding.

- The real difference is detection lag: months after the close versus days after posting.
- Rules catch known patterns, models rank what rules miss, and a person decides every finding.
- Continuous auditing sees only what was recorded, so physical counts, confirmations and judgement stay human.
- Start with one process, three to five tests and a named reviewer, then widen.

A finance manager receives the management letter in April. One point says a vendor was paid twice for the same invoice the previous May. The payment is eleven months old, the person who approved it has changed roles, and the question in the board meeting is not what happened but why nobody saw it for a year. Nothing in that audit was done badly. It was done late, by design.

That design is the subject of this comparison. The ACFE’s 2026 Report to the Nations found that the median occupational fraud lasts 12 months before it is detected, and that tips, not audits, were the top detection method in 43% of cases. The case for testing all year rather than once is made in why an annual audit misses eleven months; this article takes the AI angle and puts the two approaches side by side, so you can decide what to keep, what to change and in what order.

#### What is continuous auditing with AI?

Continuous auditing with AI is the practice of testing every ledger transaction against defined audit rules shortly after it is posted, using automated tests and AI models to rank risk, and routing each exception to a named person who reviews it against evidence. Two words carry the weight: every, and named. Coverage becomes the full population; accountability stays with a person.

It helps to separate it from continuous monitoring. Monitoring is owned by management and is part of the control itself, for example a payables supervisor who reviews a daily duplicate report. Auditing is owned by an independent function, internal audit or an outsourced provider, that tests whether those controls work. Both fit COSO’s Principle 16, which calls for ongoing and separate evaluations of internal control. For the wider map of where AI sits in finance, start with our practical guide to AI in accounting.

#### How does continuous auditing differ from a traditional audit?

| Dimension | Traditional audit | Continuous auditing with AI |
| Timing | After the period closes, once or a few times a year | Daily or after each posting run, throughout the year |
| Coverage | A sample selected under ISA 530, plus targeted items | Every transaction in the defined population, ranked by risk |
| Detection lag | Months: the error is found after the books are closed | Days: the error is found while the period is still open |
| Evidence | Documents requested and inspected during fieldwork | Ledger records with their ids, linked to source documents and stored with the finding |
| Output | An opinion (external) or a periodic report (internal) | A live exception queue, with periodic reports built from it |
| Who decides | The audit team, at the end of fieldwork | A named reviewer per exception, escalated by materiality |
| Main weakness | Sampling risk and stale findings | Alert fatigue, data quality and the quality of the test design |

Continuous auditing does not remove risk; it exchanges one kind for another. Sampling risk shrinks for the attributes you test, because nothing is left out, a shift explained in detail in our guide to moving from sampling to full-population testing. In its place come the risks of a badly designed test, an incomplete extract and a reviewer who stops reading alerts.

An external auditor still forms an opinion under the ISAs and decides how far to rely on anyone else’s work. Better internal evidence makes that reliance easier to justify, not automatic. The standards themselves are moving: in August 2026 the IAASB issued exposure drafts revising ISA 500, ISA 330 and ISA 520 to address the increased use of technology, with comments due by 15 December 2026. They are drafts, so do not build methodology on wording that may change.

#### What does AI actually do in a continuous audit?

Three layers do different jobs, and confusing them is a frequent design mistake.

##### Rules: the known patterns

Deterministic tests answer yes or no questions and run first, because they are cheap, explainable and repeatable. The patterns we find most often in continuous-audit work are:

- Duplicate and near-duplicate payments to the same vendor.
- Near-duplicate vendors: the same supplier set up twice under slightly different names.
- Approvals outside the approval matrix, including approvals by the person who raised the request, a test that depends on clean segregation of duties, including AI agents as users.
- Cut-off errors, where the document date and the posting period disagree.
- Inventory valuation drift between the valuation report and the ledger.
- Manual journal entries posted late at month-end in round amounts, the population ISA 240 expects auditors to examine when testing journal entries.

##### Models: what rules miss

A rule finds an exact duplicate. A model finds the bill that is not identical to anything but is unusual in several ways at once: a new vendor, an unusual posting hour, a user who rarely posts to that account. The output is a ranking, not a verdict. Its value is that the reviewer reads the riskiest twenty exceptions first rather than the first twenty.

##### Language: explaining and drafting

Language models are good at turning an exception into a readable draft finding and at pulling the related documents together. They are also capable of stating a number that is not in the books. The control is simple and non-negotiable: every statement in a draft must cite the records it came from, or it is rejected. We call that rule evidence or silence, explained in our article on AI provenance and the audit trail. And a flag is a question, not a conclusion; AI-based fraud detection explains why a red flag is never proof of fraud.

#### What does a continuous audit cycle look like in practice?

1. Extract new postings since the last run through a dedicated read-only API user, as described in connecting AI to Odoo for continuous auditing.
2. Reconcile the extract to the trial balance for the same period, so you know the population is complete before you test it.
3. Run the rule tests, then the model scoring, on the new population.
4. Suppress only patterns that have been explained before, and record who approved each suppression and why.
5. Assign every remaining exception to a named reviewer, who checks it against the source document.
6. Raise a finding with condition, criteria, cause, owner and due date, or close the exception with the evidence that explains it.
7. Draft any correction for a person to approve, with a second approver above the ISA 320 materiality threshold, as set out in our note on materiality thresholds.
8. Report monthly: open findings, ageing, repeats of earlier findings, and tests that produced nothing (which may mean the test is broken).

#### Where does the traditional audit still win?

A continuous test sees only what was recorded. It cannot count stock in a warehouse, obtain a bank confirmation, read the tone of a management meeting, or see a side agreement that was never entered. Accounting estimates, going concern, related parties outside the books and the plausibility of management’s explanations remain judgement work. The ACFE’s 2026 report also found that more than half of cases involved a lack of internal controls or an override of existing ones, and an override performed by someone with the right access can look perfectly normal in the data.

There is also a dependency the traditional auditor checks first and a continuous programme often forgets: the IT environment. ISA 315 (Revised 2019) requires auditors to understand general IT controls because ledger data is only as reliable as the access rights behind it. Odoo’s 20 release notes say changes to user groups are now logged in the user’s chatter, which gives a reviewer a trail of who received which access and when. Test that trail before you trust the transactions.

#### What are the risks, and how do you control them?

- Alert fatigue. Control: thresholds linked to materiality, and a weekly review of the ten most suppressed patterns.
- Incomplete data. Control: reconcile every extract to the trial balance and stop the run if it does not agree.
- Silent test failure. Control: a test that returns zero exceptions for three cycles is reviewed, not celebrated.
- Loss of independence. Control: the people who own the process do not edit the tests, and every rule change is logged with an approver.
- Invented explanations. Control: drafts without record citations are rejected and never presented as facts.
- Usage cost. If you use Odoo’s native AI, Odoo’s 20 release notes say all AI features consume IAP credits billed per request, so budget by volume of runs.

> A finding that arrives eleven months late is a history lesson, not a control.

#### Where should a finance team start on Monday?

Pick one process with high volume and clear rules, usually payables. Choose three to five tests from the list above. Run them backwards on the last closed quarter and compare the results with what your last audit sample found; that comparison calibrates thresholds and tells you which tests produce noise. Then run weekly, assign a named reviewer, and keep the working papers ISA 230 expects: what was tested, what was found and how each exception was resolved. Widen to a second process only when the first queue is being cleared on time.

This is how we run it. MFT’s seg-audit platform reads the books straight from the ERP, read-only, scores every transaction by risk instead of sampling a few percent, and keeps each finding on record with its evidence and severity; a finding cannot be closed without a named, registered approver. Our Auditor agent drafts findings and correcting entries for a person to approve, and our internal audit service supplies the licensed reviewers when you do not have them in-house.

Q: Does continuous auditing replace the external auditor?
A: No. The external auditor still forms an independent opinion under the ISAs and decides how much to rely on internal work. Continuous auditing improves the evidence available during the year and can reduce surprises at year end, but reliance is the external auditor’s judgement, not something the company can assume.

Q: What is the difference between continuous auditing and continuous monitoring?
A: Continuous monitoring is performed by management as part of a control, such as a supervisor reviewing a daily exceptions report. Continuous auditing is performed by an independent function that tests whether those controls work. Both use similar automated tests; the difference is ownership and independence.

Q: Which transactions should be tested continuously first?
A: Start where volume is high and rules are clear: vendor bills and payments, manual journal entries, and vendor master changes. These produce testable patterns such as duplicates, approvals outside the matrix and late round-amount entries, and errors there move cash out of the business quickly.

Q: Can AI-flagged exceptions be used as audit evidence?
A: The flag itself is not evidence; the ledger records and source documents behind it are. An exception becomes usable evidence when a reviewer has checked it against those records, documented the conclusion and kept the trail. Any AI statement that does not cite the underlying records should be rejected.

Q: How often should continuous audit tests run?
A: Match frequency to how quickly the risk turns into loss. Payment and vendor master tests suit daily or before each payment run; journal entry and cut-off tests suit weekly runs and the month-end close. Running more often than a reviewer can clear the queue only creates backlog.

Sources:
- ACFE, "Occupational Fraud 2026: A Report to the Nations" (press release, 19 May 2026): https://www.acfe.com/about-the-acfe/newsroom-for-media/press-releases/press-release-detail?s=report-to-the-
- IAASB, "Project update: ISA 500, Audit Evidence" (exposure drafts issued August 2026): https://www.iaasb.org/publications/project-update-isa-500-audit-evidence

### Full-population testing with AI vs audit sampling: a practical guide
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/full-population-testing-ai-vs-sampling/
Published: 2026-10-14

Full-population testing with AI means running an audit procedure on every transaction in a defined population instead of a statistical or judgemental sample. It removes sampling risk for the attributes tested, but it does not remove the need to prove the data is complete, design the right tests, and have a person evaluate each exception against evidence.

- Testing every item answers a different question from sampling: not “is the error rate acceptable?” but “which items are wrong?”
- The remaining risks are incomplete data, a badly designed test and a misjudged exception.
- Reconcile the extracted population to the trial balance before running any test.
- Sampling still has a place where evidence is physical, external or costly per item.

An audit senior opens the payables population for the year: several thousand vendor bills. The plan calls for a few dozen items, selected with care and documented properly. The sample comes back clean, and the file says so. In the same population, two bills from the same vendor carry the same reference a week apart, and neither was selected. The sample was correct. It was also silent about the two items that mattered.

Sampling exists because, for most of audit history, testing everything was impossible within any sensible budget. That constraint has largely gone for anything held in a ledger. The question is no longer whether you can test every transaction, but what changes in your method, your evidence and your judgement when you do. This guide answers that, with a worked procedure you can run on your own data.

#### What is full-population testing?

Full-population testing is applying an audit procedure to every item in a defined population, such as all vendor bills posted in a year, rather than to a selected subset. ISA 530 governs audit sampling, where the auditor applies procedures to less than the whole population and draws a conclusion about the rest. When every item is tested, there is no extrapolation and therefore no sampling risk for that test. What remains is the risk that the population is incomplete, that the test is wrong, or that someone misreads an exception.

Definition is half the work. “All purchases” is not a population; “all posted vendor bills and credit notes in the purchase journals between two dates, for all companies in the database” is. If the definition is loose, the test is complete only for the part you happened to extract. Full-population testing is one of the engines of continuous auditing with AI, and the series hub on AI in accounting shows where it fits among the other uses.

#### How is it different from audit sampling under ISA 530?

| Aspect | Audit sampling (ISA 530) | Full-population testing with AI |
| Question answered | Is the error rate or misstatement in the population acceptable? | Which specific items fail the test? |
| Risk that remains | Sampling risk plus non-sampling risk | Non-sampling risk only: wrong test, incomplete data, misjudged exception |
| Completeness check | Population defined, then sampled | Extracted population reconciled to the ledger before testing |
| Exceptions | Few, each investigated, then projected | Many, ranked by risk, each resolved or explained |
| Documentation (ISA 230) | Selection method, items tested, results, projection | Test logic, population totals, every exception and its resolution |
| Effort profile | Spread across document inspection | Concentrated in test design and exception review |
| Best suited to | Physical, external or costly-per-item evidence | Attributes visible in ledger and system data |

The first row is the one people miss. Sampling estimates; full-population testing identifies. That changes what you do with the result. A projected error is evaluated against materiality as a whole. An identified exception is a specific record with a specific owner, and it needs a specific resolution.

#### Does testing 100% of transactions mean 100% assurance?

No, and claiming it would be a documentation problem waiting to happen. A test detects only what it was designed to detect. A duplicate test on reference numbers will not find a duplicate entered with a different reference. A cut-off test on dates will not find a sale that should never have been recorded. ISA 500 asks whether information used as audit evidence is relevant and reliable, and that applies to the extract and the test logic as much as to any document. The IAASB’s August 2026 exposure drafts revising ISA 500, ISA 330 and ISA 520 address the increased use of technology; comments are due by 15 December 2026 and the drafts are not yet final, so watch the wording rather than anticipate it.

A decision rule we use: describe a full-population test by the attribute it proves and the population it covers, never as “all transactions tested”. “Every posted vendor bill in the year was tested for duplicate vendor and reference” is a claim you can defend. “AP was tested 100%” is not.

#### How does AI help test a full population?

##### Preparing the data

Before any test, profile the population: count of records, totals by period, blank fields, users who posted, posting dates outside the period. Then reconcile totals to the trial balance. AI is useful here for spotting inconsistent text, such as one vendor written five ways, but the reconciliation itself is arithmetic and should stay deterministic.

##### Testing and ranking

Rules test attributes: duplicates, approvals, dates, round amounts. Models then rank all items by risk so that reviewers start at the top rather than in posting order. Ranking is what makes a full population workable: a reviewer cannot read every line, but can read the riskiest ones first and document why the rest were not escalated.

##### Documenting

Language models can draft the exception narrative and the working paper. The safeguard is that every statement cites the records it was drawn from; anything else is rejected. That principle, evidence or silence, is covered in our article on AI provenance and the audit trail.

#### A worked example: testing every vendor bill in a quarter

The procedure below uses no amounts. It can be run on any ERP; where Odoo features are mentioned, confirm them in your own database and edition.

1. Define the population: all posted vendor bills and credit notes in the purchase journals for the quarter, for every company in scope.
2. Reconcile: the count and total of the extract must agree with the movement on the payables control account for the same period. If they do not, stop and find the gap.
3. Test exact duplicates: same vendor, same reference, same amount. Odoo’s 20 release notes add duplicate detection on invoices and bills with two levels, red for highly likely and yellow for potential duplicates; compare your results with those warnings to learn whether the system control is working.
4. Test near-duplicates: same vendor and amount within a short date window but a different reference, and vendors whose names differ only slightly.
5. Test approvals: bills linked to purchase orders that exceeded the approval threshold without a manager’s validation. In recent Odoo versions this rests on the Purchase Order Approval setting; confirm how it is configured in your 20 database, and see three-way match purchase controls for the matching side.
6. Test segregation: the same user created the vendor, raised the order and validated the bill, a pattern explored in AI and segregation of duties.
7. Test cut-off: bill date and posting period disagree around the quarter end.
8. Rank all exceptions by risk and review from the top, recording the conclusion for each.

#### How should exceptions be evaluated?

Every exception ends in one of four categories, and the category decides what happens next.

- Explained: a legitimate item, such as a recurring monthly bill. Record the evidence that explains it and consider refining the test.
- Control deviation: the control did not operate, but no misstatement resulted. Report it as a control finding with an owner.
- Misstatement: the books are wrong. Quantify it, evaluate it against materiality as described in our note on ISA 320 thresholds, and correct it by reversal, never by deletion.
- Fraud indicator: an item that calls for the inquiries ISA 240 requires. It is not proof; AI-based fraud detection explains why a flag is a question, not a conclusion.

> Testing every transaction removes sampling risk. It does not remove the duty to be right about what you tested.

#### When is sampling still the right tool?

When the evidence is not in the system. Physical inventory, external confirmations, inspection of a signed contract or a site visit cost the same per item whether or not you have AI, so sampling remains the rational choice. The two approaches also combine well: use the full population to identify high-risk strata, test those strata fully, and sample the low-risk remainder where documentary evidence is needed. The ACFE’s 2024 Report to the Nations found that proactive data monitoring and analysis was among the anti-fraud controls associated with roughly half the losses and duration, which argues for running analytics across the population, not for abandoning judgement about where to look closer.

#### Where to start on Monday

Choose one population you already sample, most often payables. Define it precisely, reconcile it to the trial balance, and run the five tests from the worked example on the last closed quarter. Then compare: what did the full-population tests find that the last sample did not, and how many exceptions turned out to be explained items? That comparison is your calibration, and your first working paper.

This is the method behind MFT’s seg-audit platform, which reads the books from the ERP read-only and scores every transaction by risk instead of sampling a few percent. Every finding has a source in the books, is classified against the ISAs, and keeps an evidence trail that external auditors can use. If you want the analysis run for you, our internal audit service and the Auditor agent, which drafts findings for a named person to approve, are where to start.

Q: Is full-population testing allowed under ISA 530?
A: ISA 530 governs audit sampling, which applies when procedures cover less than the whole population. Testing every item is not sampling, so there is no sampling risk to evaluate for that test. The other standards still apply: the data must be reliable under ISA 500 and the work documented under ISA 230.

Q: Does 100% testing mean the auditor finds every error?
A: No. A full-population test finds only the errors it was designed to find, in the data that was extracted. Errors of a different type, transactions never recorded, and items outside the defined population remain undetected. Describe each test by the attribute and the population it covers.

Q: How do you handle thousands of exceptions from full-population testing?
A: Rank exceptions by risk, review from the top, and refine tests that produce mostly explained items. Suppress a recurring pattern only with a recorded reason and approver. A queue that nobody can clear is a design problem in the tests, not a reason to return to sampling.

Q: What data do I need to start full-population testing?
A: A complete extract of the population with record ids, dates, users, vendors or customers, references, amounts and approval data, plus the trial balance for the same period. Reconcile the extract to the ledger first; without that reconciliation, the test is complete only for the data you happened to receive.

Q: Can external auditors rely on full-population tests run by the company?
A: They can consider them, but reliance is their decision. They will want to understand the data source, how completeness was checked, the logic of each test, and how exceptions were resolved. A documented trail from each finding back to the ledger records makes that evaluation much easier.

Sources:
- IAASB, "Project update: ISA 500, Audit Evidence" (exposure drafts issued August 2026): https://www.iaasb.org/publications/project-update-isa-500-audit-evidence
- ACFE, "Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations" (report, 2024): https://www.acfe.com/en-us/-/media/files/acfe/pdfs/rttn/2024/2024-report-to-the-nations.pdf

### AI and segregation of duties: internal controls when agents are users
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/ai-segregation-of-duties-internal-controls/
Published: 2026-10-14

AI changes segregation of duties because an AI agent that can create or update accounting records is, for control purposes, a user. It must sit in the SoD matrix with a role, an owner and minimum rights. Keep its output in draft for a named person to approve, and use AI to test conflicts across every transaction.

- An agent that can create or update records performs the recording function and belongs in the SoD matrix.
- Agents may draft, propose and monitor; authorization and custody stay with named people.
- AI adds configuration conflicts: the person who writes an agent’s instructions should not approve its drafts.
- Used as a detective control, AI checks who actually did what on every transaction, not who could have.

Run a user access review on an ERP where AI has been on for a few months and a new kind of line appears. It is not a person, it has no job description, it was set up by IT or the implementation partner, and it can create and update records in Accounting. Nobody put it in the segregation of duties matrix, because the matrix was written for people.

The basics of conflicting duties in Odoo are in our guide to segregation of duties in Odoo. This article asks what changes when some hands in a process are agents, and how the same technology can test segregation on every transaction. It is part of our series on AI in accounting in 2026.

#### What is segregation of duties when AI is part of the process?

Segregation of duties is the design rule that no single user, human or automated, can authorize, record, hold custody of and reconcile the same transaction. The four functions have not changed; the list of users has. COSO’s Internal Control, Integrated Framework (2013) has a place for this: Principle 10 covers control activities such as segregation, and Principle 11 covers general controls over technology, which is where the configuration of an AI agent belongs. ISA 315 (Revised 2019) requires the external auditor to understand the IT environment and general IT controls, so an agent with write access will be in scope at your next audit whether you mapped it or not.

#### Is an AI agent a "user" for segregation of duties?

For control purposes, yes: the test is whether the actor can change the books. According to Odoo’s 20 release notes, AI agents can create records (including from an uploaded instruction file such as a PDF), update records, and be triggered by automated actions and scheduled actions. Anything that can create or update an accounting record performs the recording function and must sit in the matrix with a role, an owner and limits.

Before designing anything, confirm in your own Odoo 20 database under whose access rights an agent’s actions run and how its changes are attributed in the record history; that decides whether a conflict sits with the agent, the person who triggered it, or both. Also confirm which AI features your edition and plan include. Every AI request consumes IAP credits, billed per request and not included in any plan.

##### Decision rule: which of the four functions may an agent hold?

| Function | May an AI agent hold it? | Condition |
| Authorize | No | Approval is a judgment that carries accountability, so it stays with a named, registered person. An agent may prepare the approval file. |
| Record | Draft only | The agent drafts entries or records; a person who did not configure the agent reviews and posts them. |
| Custody | No | No agent should initiate payments. If you pay bills from Odoo through payment initiation (PISP), keep the release with a person. |
| Reconcile | Propose only | The agent proposes matches and flags suspected errors; a person validates the reconciliation. |
| Monitor | Yes | Reading the full population for exceptions is where AI adds most and conflicts least, provided findings go to someone independent. |

#### Which conflicts does AI introduce that a classic SoD matrix misses?

AI adds conflicting pairs that sit in configuration, not in transactions, so a classic matrix misses them:

- Agent configurer and approver. Whoever writes an agent’s instructions and skills shapes every entry it drafts. In Odoo 20, "topics" are renamed "skills" and default prompts accept context and dynamic values, so a one-line change can alter a month of drafts. That person should not approve them.
- Requester and approver of the same run. The person who asks an agent to prepare a correcting entry should not be the one who approves it.
- Trigger owner and process owner. Agents can be fired by automated and scheduled actions, and Studio automation rules can now trigger activity plans. Changing a trigger is changing a control, so it needs change management.
- Button clicker and authority holder. Odoo 20 agents ask questions, request permission and make suggestions answered by buttons, and they ask before exceeding their tool call limit. Each click is an approval, so define who may click.
- Connection owner and data owner. The release notes describe connecting to the database via MCP. An external connection is a user with rights; it belongs in the matrix and in your design for connecting AI to Odoo.

#### How do you design internal controls for AI agents in Odoo?

Treat each agent like a new team member who works fast, never tires and has no judgment. Our procedure:

1. Inventory every agent, every automated or scheduled action that calls AI, and every API or MCP connection. Record its owner, its trigger and the models it can create or update.
2. Map each one to the four functions and add it to the SoD matrix as its own row, next to the people.
3. Set its access rights to the minimum. Odoo’s 20 release notes say record rules are removed and the domain is set directly on the access right, so any restriction you relied on before an upgrade must be re-checked, not assumed.
4. Keep agent output in draft. A named person who did not configure the agent posts it. Confirm in your database that the agent’s rights do not allow posting or confirming.
5. Tier approvals by materiality: above your ISA 320 materiality threshold, require a second approver.
6. Correct by reversal, never by deletion, and protect closed periods with lock dates (long-standing in recent Odoo versions; confirm in your 20 database who can change them).
7. Retain evidence outside the chat. Stored AI conversations are kept up to 30 days after the last message, so anything you need as audit evidence must be captured in the record or a working paper before then.
8. Review agent rights and configuration every quarter, using the user group change log that Odoo 20 keeps in each user’s chatter.

The governance of the agents themselves is covered in Odoo 20 AI agents under finance controls, and the principle behind step 4 is set out in agents draft, people approve.

> An agent that can write to the ledger is a user. Give it a role, an owner, and a person who signs for its work.

#### How can AI test segregation of duties instead of threatening it?

A manual access review checks who could act. A data test checks who did act, on every transaction. The difference matters: the ACFE’s Occupational Fraud 2026 report found that more than half of cases involved a lack of internal controls or an override of existing ones, and that proactive data monitoring is associated with lower losses and faster detection.

| Risk | Preventive control | Detective test on the full population | Evidence to retain |
| Fictitious vendor paid | Vendor maintenance and payment release in different roles | Same user changed a vendor’s bank details and released a payment to that vendor | Vendor change log, payment record, user ids |
| Self-approved journal entry | Posting and approval in different roles | Same user created and posted a manual entry, especially late in the month and in round amounts | Entry history with creator and poster |
| Approval bypass | Purchase Order Approval above a set amount (recent Odoo versions; confirm in 20) | Orders confirmed outside the approval matrix, or split to fall just below the threshold | Order approval history, version of the approval matrix |
| Duplicate payment | Duplicate detection warnings on bills | Duplicate and near-duplicate payments, near-duplicate vendors | Bill ids, payment ids, warning status |
| Agent drift | Draft-only rights; approval by someone other than the configurer | Drafts approved by the person who configured or triggered the agent | Agent configuration history, approver id |

Running these tests on every record is the subject of full-population testing with AI. A hit is a lead, not a finding: two conflicting roles held by one user is a design weakness, and whether it was exploited is a question for evidence, as explained in AI-based fraud detection.

#### What if the team is too small to separate duties?

A two-person team cannot split seven conflicting pairs, and agents do not change that, because an agent cannot carry accountability. The answer is still compensating controls, now cheaper to run. An owner or general manager outside the transaction reviews a short monthly exception list produced by AI: users who both created and approved, vendor bank changes followed by payments, manual entries after the close. The review is quick because the list is short, and documented because the list is a record. That is COSO Principle 16 (ongoing and separate evaluations) in a form a small team can sustain.

#### Where to start on Monday

1. List every AI agent, automation and external connection in your ERP, with one named owner for each.
2. Add them as rows in your SoD matrix and mark the function each one performs.
3. Remove posting, confirming and payment rights from agents; keep them on draft.
4. Run one detective test on the last quarter: users who both created and approved the same journal entry or vendor payment.
5. Agree who reviews the exceptions, and how evidence is kept beyond the 30-day conversation window.

This is how we built MFT Intelligence, twelve finance agents written by MFT’s accountants: agents draft correcting entries and adjustments, a named, registered person approves, a second approver is required above the client’s ISA 320 materiality threshold, corrections are made by reversal, and nothing is auto-posted. The Auditor agent is available now as a managed service, and our internal audit team can bring your agents into a segregation of duties review alongside your people. See also the AI audit trail and continuous auditing with AI.

Q: Can an AI agent approve transactions in an ERP?
A: It should not. Approval carries accountability, and an agent cannot be held accountable. Let the agent prepare the approval file, such as the supporting records and the exceptions it found, and leave the decision to a named, registered person. Above your materiality threshold, add a second approver who did not request the agent’s work.

Q: Who should configure AI agents in the finance system?
A: Someone who does not approve what the agent produces. Writing an agent’s instructions shapes every draft it creates, so it is a recording function. Separate it from approval, put configuration changes under change management, and review the configuration history at least quarterly alongside user access rights.

Q: How does AI help test segregation of duties?
A: It reads every transaction instead of a sample and checks who actually acted: the same user creating and posting a journal entry, changing a vendor’s bank details and releasing a payment, or approving outside the approval matrix. Each hit is a lead for review, documented with record ids, not a confirmed violation.

Q: Does Odoo 20 change access rights for segregation of duties?
A: According to Odoo’s 20 release notes, record rules are removed and the domain is set directly on the access right, and user group changes are logged in the user’s chatter. After upgrading, re-test every restriction your segregation design relied on and use the change log as review evidence.

Q: Is a segregation of duties conflict found by AI proof of fraud?
A: No. A conflict shows that one user could, or did, perform two functions that should be separate. That is a control weakness. Whether anyone misused it is a separate question answered by examining the underlying transactions and documents, with the person involved given a chance to explain.

- Odoo, "Odoo 20 Release Notes" (24 September 2026): https://www.odoo.com/odoo-20-release-notes
